options.a: Visible chest rise with each ventilation
options.b: A pulse oximeter reading that rises within seconds
options.c: Resistance felt in the bag as each breath is squeezed
options.d: Abdomen rising and falling with each ventilation

distractorExplanations.b: SpO2 lags behind ventilation by a minute or more and can mislead with poor perfusion or CO; chest rise is the immediate sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising bag resistance suggests airway obstruction, gastric distension, or poor lung compliance, not effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal rise means air is entering the stomach (gastric insufflation) from excess volume or poor head position.

options.a: Place in the recovery position and observe breathing closely
options.b: Support ventilation with BVM/oxygen and consider naloxone
options.c: Give naloxone and wait for breathing to improve on its own
options.d: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and monitor

distractorExplanations.a: The recovery position protects the airway but does not fix slow, shallow breathing; ventilations must be assisted.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone takes minutes to act; inadequate ventilation is supported with a BVM first rather than waiting.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonrebreather requires adequate spontaneous breathing; slow, shallow respirations need assisted BVM ventilation.

options.a: Bronchoconstriction of the lower airways
options.b: Fluid in the alveoli from acute pulmonary edema
options.c: Complete obstruction with no air movement
options.d: Partial obstruction at or above the larynx

distractorExplanations.a: Lower-airway narrowing produces expiratory wheezing, not the inspiratory stridor of an upper airway obstruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Alveolar fluid produces crackles (rales), not the high-pitched inspiratory sound of stridor.
distractorExplanations.c: Complete obstruction is silent; stridor requires air moving past a partial narrowing.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: Stridor is a hallmark of upper airway narrowing and is an emergency warning sign. It produces a high-pitched inspiratory sound.

options.a: Limit suction attempts to about 15 seconds
options.b: Suction while inserting the catheter to clear more fluid
options.c: Insert the rigid tip past the base of the tongue
options.d: Limit suction attempts to about 30 seconds in adults

distractorExplanations.b: Suction is applied only while withdrawing the catheter; suctioning on insertion worsens hypoxia and mucosal trauma.
distractorExplanations.c: A rigid catheter is inserted only as far as you can see; passing the base of the tongue triggers gagging and a vagal response.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty seconds is twice the adult limit; prolonged suction causes hypoxia and bradycardia.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: Prolonged suction causes hypoxia; clear the airway in brief attempts. Preoxygenate as able before and between attempts.

options.a: It pushes the tongue back into the airway
options.b: It may worsen cervical spine injury
options.c: It raises intracranial pressure in head injuries
options.d: It is less effective than the jaw-thrust

distractorExplanations.a: The maneuver lifts the tongue off the pharynx; the trauma concern is neck extension worsening a spinal injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Airway positioning does not meaningfully raise ICP; the concern is spinal movement from neck extension.
distractorExplanations.d: The head-tilt/chin-lift is usually the more effective maneuver; it is avoided in trauma because of neck extension, not efficacy.

options.a: Upper airway swelling at the larynx
options.b: Fluid in the alveoli of the lungs
options.c: Lower airway bronchoconstriction
options.d: Collapse of a lung from pneumothorax

distractorExplanations.a: Laryngeal swelling causes high-pitched inspiratory stridor, not the expiratory wheezing of narrowed bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.b: Alveolar fluid produces crackles (rales); wheezing comes from narrowed lower airways.
distractorExplanations.d: Pneumothorax causes diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side, not wheezing.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: Expiratory wheeze reflects narrowed lower airways; still assess for other causes. Asthma and COPD exacerbations are the classic causes.

options.a: High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather at 15 L/min
options.b: CPAP at low pressure to improve oxygenation and lung expansion
options.c: A nasopharyngeal airway with blow-by oxygen
options.d: Assisted positive-pressure ventilation (e.g., BVM)

distractorExplanations.a: A nonrebreather adds oxygen but does not move air; inadequate rate or depth requires assisted ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: CPAP needs an alert patient who breathes adequately on their own; inadequate breathing calls for BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: An NPA keeps the airway open but does not ventilate, and blow-by oxygen cannot correct poor ventilation.

options.a: Respiratory distress from conditions like CHF/pulmonary edema
options.b: Respiratory distress from a suspected tension pneumothorax
options.c: Inadequate breathing with a decreased level of responsiveness
options.d: Respiratory distress with systolic BP below 90 mm Hg

distractorExplanations.b: Positive pressure can enlarge a pneumothorax; suspected pneumothorax is a CPAP contraindication.
distractorExplanations.c: CPAP needs an alert patient who protects their airway and breathes adequately; this patient needs BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypotension is a CPAP contraindication because positive pressure reduces venous return and cardiac output.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: CPAP requires a spontaneously breathing cooperative patient; not for arrest or complete obstruction. It stents the airways open and improves oxygenation.

options.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning
options.b: Significant hypoxemia
options.c: Severe anemia with normal SpO2
options.d: Peripheral vasodilation

distractorExplanations.a: CO poisoning typically does not cause cyanosis; skin color and pulse oximetry can look falsely normal.
distractorExplanations.c: Anemia causes pallor; cyanosis needs enough deoxygenated hemoglobin, which anemic patients may lack.
distractorExplanations.d: Vasodilation causes flushed, red skin; the bluish color of cyanosis reflects deoxygenated hemoglobin.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: Central cyanosis is a late, serious sign of poor oxygenation. It calls for urgent airway, oxygen, and ventilation assessment.

options.a: The attack is resolving as the bronchospasm eases
options.b: Drowsiness as an expected side effect of nebulized albuterol
options.c: Worsening obstruction and impending respiratory failure
options.d: Hyperventilation from anxiety lowering CO2 levels

distractorExplanations.a: Less wheezing with drowsiness and poor air movement means too little airflow to wheeze — a silent chest, not recovery.
distractorExplanations.b: Albuterol causes tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety, not sedation; drowsiness here signals exhaustion.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilation causes rapid breathing and tingling, not drowsiness with poor air movement.

options.a: Head-tilt/chin-lift once a rigid cervical collar is applied
options.b: Sniffing position with the head slightly extended back
options.c: Jaw-thrust after log-rolling the patient onto one side
options.d: Jaw-thrust while maintaining manual cervical stabilization

distractorExplanations.a: A collar does not prevent the extension of a head-tilt; jaw-thrust with manual stabilization is used instead.
distractorExplanations.b: The sniffing position extends the neck; it is for non-trauma airway positioning, not suspected c-spine injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolling before manual stabilization moves the spine; the jaw-thrust is done with the head held inline in the position found.

options.a: About 1 breath every 5–6 seconds (roughly 10–12/min)
options.b: As fast as possible until the SpO2 reaches 100%
options.c: About 1 breath every 10–12 seconds (roughly 5–6/min)
options.d: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, as in adult CPR

distractorExplanations.b: Rapid ventilation causes hyperventilation, gastric inflation, and reduced venous return; aim for 10–12 per minute.
distractorExplanations.c: Five to six breaths per minute under-ventilates an adult with a pulse; deliver one breath every 5–6 seconds.
distractorExplanations.d: 30:2 is the CPR ratio for a pulseless patient; a patient with a pulse receives rescue breaths without compressions.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: Avoid hyperventilation; deliver breaths that produce chest rise at an appropriate rate. Each breath should be just enough to produce visible chest rise.

options.a: No more than about 5 seconds per adult attempt
options.b: No more than about 15 seconds per attempt
options.c: No more than about 30 seconds per attempt
options.d: One attempt, then switch to finger sweeps

distractorExplanations.a: Five seconds is the infant limit; adults can be suctioned for up to about 15 seconds per attempt.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty seconds doubles the adult limit and causes hypoxia and vagal bradycardia.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeated brief suction passes with reoxygenation are acceptable; blind finger sweeps can push material deeper.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: Brief suction clears the airway; prolonged suction worsens hypoxia—reoxygenate between attempts. Monitor oxygenation during and between attempts.

options.a: The patient is apneic and needs artificial ventilation
options.b: A COPD patient needs precise low-flow oxygen titration
options.c: A breathing patient needs high-concentration oxygen
options.d: A stable patient with SpO2 of 93% needs mild supplementation

distractorExplanations.b: Precise FiO2 titration is the job of a Venturi mask; a nonrebreather delivers high, non-adjustable concentrations.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild hypoxemia in a stable patient is usually titrated with a nasal cannula toward 94%; the NRB is for high-concentration needs.
distractorExplanations.a: Apnea requires positive-pressure ventilation.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-airway-respira.explanation: NRB delivers high FiO2 to spontaneously breathing patients; apneic patients need BVM/advanced airway support. The patient must also be able to tolerate the mask.

options.a: Begin high-quality CPR and apply AED as soon as available
options.b: Give 2 rescue breaths and recheck the pulse for 1 minute
options.c: Give rescue breaths at 1 every 6 seconds without compressions
options.d: Check blood glucose before starting compressions

distractorExplanations.b: Compressions start immediately (C-A-B), and pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds in a suspected arrest.
distractorExplanations.c: Rescue breathing alone is for a patient with a pulse; a pulseless patient needs chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversible causes such as hypoglycemia are considered after compressions and defibrillation are underway.

options.a: About 1.5 inches (4 cm)
options.b: At least 2 inches (5 cm)
options.c: At least 3 inches (7.5 cm)
options.d: One-half of the chest's depth

distractorExplanations.a: About 1.5 inches is the infant compression depth; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.c: Depths beyond about 2.4 inches (6 cm) increase injury risk without benefit; the adult target is 2–2.4 inches.
distractorExplanations.d: Half the AP depth is far too deep; adults need 2–2.4 inches, and children about one-third of the AP depth.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-cardiology-res.explanation: AHA-aligned adult depth is at least 2 inches with full recoil and adequate rate. Allow full chest recoil after each compression.

options.a: Check a carotid pulse for 10 seconds before shocking
options.b: Resume CPR for 2 minutes, then shock at the next analysis
options.c: Ensure no one is touching the patient, deliver the shock
options.d: Keep compressing while the AED delivers the shock

distractorExplanations.a: A pulse check delays defibrillation; once the AED advises a shock, clear the patient and shock without a pulse check.
distractorExplanations.b: An advised shock is delivered now; delaying it lowers the chance of converting VF or pulseless VT.
distractorExplanations.d: Touching the patient during the shock risks injuring the rescuer; everyone is cleared before shocking.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-cardiology-res.explanation: Clear, shock, then immediate CPR minimizes interruptions. Then immediately resume CPR.

options.a: Dissolves existing coronary clots like a fibrinolytic in the field
options.b: Dilates coronary arteries to relieve the chest pain
options.c: Relieves cardiac pain as an analgesic at this low dose
options.d: Inhibits platelet aggregation and may limit clot progression

distractorExplanations.a: Aspirin does not lyse formed clots; fibrinolytic drugs do that in the hospital.
distractorExplanations.b: Coronary vasodilation is the action of nitroglycerin; aspirin is given as an antiplatelet agent.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-dose (162–324 mg) aspirin is given for its antiplatelet effect, not analgesia; pain relief comes from nitro or opioids.

options.a: The patient has used a PDE-5 inhibitor recently or has hypotension
options.b: The patient has chest pain that started more than 12 hours ago
options.c: The patient's systolic blood pressure is 150 mm Hg with a headache
options.d: The patient already chewed 324 mg of aspirin for this episode

distractorExplanations.b: Symptom duration does not contraindicate nitroglycerin; contraindications are low BP and recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.
distractorExplanations.c: A systolic of 150 is above the hypotension cutoff (about 90–100 mm Hg); headache is a common side effect, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.d: Aspirin and nitroglycerin are given together in suspected ACS; prior aspirin is not a contraindication.

options.a: Crackles in both lungs and pink, frothy sputum
options.b: Peripheral edema and JVD from systemic congestion
options.c: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
options.d: Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness

distractorExplanations.a: Pulmonary edema signs reflect left-sided failure backing up into the lungs, not systemic congestion.
distractorExplanations.c: Orthopnea and PND come from pulmonary congestion in left-sided heart failure.
distractorExplanations.d: One swollen, tender calf suggests deep vein thrombosis, not the bilateral edema of right heart failure.

options.a: Asystole on the monitor after two minutes of CPR
options.b: A sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 readings
options.c: Fixed, dilated pupils after resuscitation
options.d: Return of organized pulse after arrest care

distractorExplanations.a: Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity, the opposite of returning circulation.
distractorExplanations.b: ROSC typically causes an abrupt rise in ETCO2; a drop suggests poor perfusion or a displaced airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed, dilated pupils indicate poor cerebral perfusion and do not signal returning circulation.

options.a: Possible acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise
options.b: Musculoskeletal strain unless the ECG is abnormal
options.c: A panic attack if the patient is young and anxious
options.d: Acid reflux if the pain began within an hour after a large meal

distractorExplanations.b: A normal or unavailable ECG does not exclude ACS; classic radiating pressure is treated as cardiac.
distractorExplanations.c: Anxiety can coexist with ACS; radiating pressure must be managed as cardiac until ruled out.
distractorExplanations.d: Meal timing does not rule out ACS; GI causes are diagnoses of exclusion made in the hospital.

options.a: Ventricular tachycardia in an alert patient with a strong pulse
options.b: Pulseless ventricular fibrillation / ventricular tachycardia
options.c: Pulseless electrical activity and asystole on the monitor
options.d: Unresponsive patients with a slow pulse and poor perfusion

distractorExplanations.a: VT with a pulse is not an AED indication; AEDs are applied only to unresponsive, pulseless patients.
distractorExplanations.c: PEA and asystole are non-shockable rhythms; they are treated with CPR, not defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.d: Symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse is not shockable; it needs ventilation support and ALS, not defibrillation.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-cardiology-res.explanation: AEDs shock shockable arrest rhythms; pulsed patients are not defibrillated. These are the shockable rhythms.

options.a: About 1 inch (2.5 cm) with full chest recoil
options.b: About 1.5 inches (4 cm) with full chest recoil
options.c: At least 2 inches (5 cm) with full chest recoil
options.d: At least 3 inches (7.5 cm) with full chest recoil

distractorExplanations.a: One inch is far too shallow to generate blood flow in an adult; the target is at least 2 inches.
distractorExplanations.b: About 1.5 inches is the infant compression depth; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.d: Depths beyond about 2.4 inches (6 cm) increase injury risk; the adult target is 2–2.4 inches.

options.a: Check a carotid pulse for 10 seconds, then resume CPR
options.b: Reanalyze the rhythm right away to confirm the shock worked
options.c: Remove the pads and begin rescue breathing only
options.d: Resume CPR immediately for about 2 minutes, then reanalyze

distractorExplanations.a: Post-shock pulse checks delay compressions; CPR resumes immediately and the pulse is checked at the next analysis.
distractorExplanations.b: Immediate reanalysis interrupts compressions; the AED reanalyzes after 2 minutes of CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Pads stay on for repeat analysis, and the patient needs full CPR, not breaths alone, after the shock.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-cardiology-res.explanation: Post-shock CPR minimizes interruptions; AEDs prompt the next analyze cycle. Follow the AED prompts for the next analysis.

options.a: Peripheral edema and jugular venous distention
options.b: Crackles in both lungs and pink frothy sputum
options.c: Unilateral calf swelling with tenderness and warmth
options.d: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea at night

distractorExplanations.b: Pulmonary edema signs point to left-sided failure backing up into the lungs, not systemic right-sided congestion.
distractorExplanations.c: One swollen, tender, warm calf suggests deep vein thrombosis, not the bilateral dependent edema of right heart failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Orthopnea and PND reflect pulmonary congestion from left-sided failure rather than systemic venous congestion.

options.a: Dissolves established fibrin clots like fibrinolytics in the field
options.b: Inhibits platelet aggregation and may reduce clot progression
options.c: Dilates coronary arteries to relieve the chest pain quickly
options.d: Relieves cardiac pain as an analgesic at this low dose

distractorExplanations.c: Coronary vasodilation is the action of nitroglycerin; aspirin is given as an antiplatelet agent.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-dose (162–324 mg) aspirin is given for its antiplatelet effect, not analgesia; pain relief comes from nitro or opioids.
distractorExplanations.a: EMTs do not give field fibrinolytics as aspirin’s role.

options.a: Assume death because no pulse is palpable
options.b: Place AED pads directly over the device driveline
options.c: Follow local VAD/cardiac arrest protocols
options.d: Disconnect the device power to reset its alarms

distractorExplanations.a: Continuous-flow VADs often produce no palpable pulse; absence of a pulse alone does not confirm arrest or death.
distractorExplanations.b: Pads are placed away from the device and driveline; placing them over hardware can damage the pump.
distractorExplanations.d: Disconnecting power stops the pump; controllers stay connected and troubleshooting follows the VAD team's guidance.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-cardiology-res.explanation: VAD patients need specialized protocols; lack of palpable pulse may be expected—use device assessment cues and local rules. This often means CPR if indicated and contacting medical direction or the device coordinator.

options.a: Find and fix life threats first
options.b: Complete a SAMPLE history before any exam
options.c: Splint long-bone fractures before moving on
options.d: Transport only after full secondary survey

distractorExplanations.b: SAMPLE history belongs to the secondary assessment, after immediate life threats are addressed.
distractorExplanations.c: Splinting is part of secondary care; airway, breathing, and bleeding control come first.
distractorExplanations.d: Load-and-go may interrupt full secondary survey.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-001.explanation: XABC/ABC priorities address immediate killers first. Threats to airway, breathing, and circulation come first.

options.a: Bulky gauze dressing packed into the wound
options.b: Occlusive dressing sealed on three sides
options.c: Pressure dressing wrapped tightly around the chest
options.d: Needle decompression of the chest by the EMT

distractorExplanations.a: Gauze lets air pass through; an open chest wound needs an occlusive (airtight) seal.
distractorExplanations.c: A tight circumferential wrap restricts chest expansion and does not seal the wound against air entry.
distractorExplanations.d: Needle decompression is beyond EMT scope and treats tension pneumothorax, not initial open-wound care.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-002.explanation: Three-sided occlusive dressing can prevent air entry while allowing escape; monitor for tension. A commercial vented chest seal may be used per protocol.

options.a: Elevation and pressure-point compression
options.b: A loose dressing with the patient in shock position
options.c: Direct pressure and tourniquet use when indicated
options.d: Tourniquet only after 10 minutes of failed pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended for life-threatening bleeding; use pressure, then a tourniquet.
distractorExplanations.b: A loose dressing does not stop arterial flow, and Trendelenburg positioning is not a hemorrhage control method.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying a tourniquet for a fixed time wastes blood; apply it as soon as pressure fails or bleeding is clearly massive.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-003.explanation: Massive hemorrhage control is a top trauma priority; tourniquets save lives in extremity bleeding. Tourniquets are used for extremity bleeding.

options.a: Stabilize pelvis per protocol and treat for shock
options.b: Compress and rock the iliac crests to confirm instability
options.c: Apply a traction splint to the leg on the injured side
options.d: Elevate the legs in shock position before stabilizing

distractorExplanations.b: Repeated rocking or springing of the pelvis can dislodge clots and worsen bleeding; it is not used to confirm a fracture.
distractorExplanations.c: Traction splints are contraindicated with pelvic fractures because the device pushes against the ischium and pelvis.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising the legs moves the fractured pelvis and delays stabilization; immobilize the pelvis first and limit movement.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-005.explanation: Pelvic fractures can cause massive bleeding; minimize movement and stabilize. Avoid excessive log-rolling.

options.a: The patient's pain level as a severity measure
options.b: Rule of Nines for BSA percentage
options.c: Parkland formula for BSA percentage
options.d: Counting blisters to set the burn depth

distractorExplanations.a: Full-thickness burns may be painless; pain level does not reflect burn size or severity.
distractorExplanations.c: The Parkland formula calculates IV fluid needs from TBSA; it does not estimate burn size.
distractorExplanations.d: Blister count does not estimate size; size is estimated by the Rule of Nines or palm method.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-006.explanation: TBSA estimation guides fluid/transport decisions along with depth and location. Age-appropriate alternatives are used for children.

options.a: Removed, then the wound packed with gauze
options.b: Removed if bleeding soaks through the bulky dressing
options.c: Stabilized in place and not removed in the field
options.d: Cut flush with the skin to ease transport

distractorExplanations.a: Removal can release a tamponaded vessel and cause severe bleeding; the object is stabilized in place.
distractorExplanations.b: Increased bleeding is controlled with pressure around the object; removal can worsen hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.d: Cutting transmits motion into the wound; an object is shortened only if needed, by rescuers, while stabilized.

options.a: Low BP, distended neck veins, muffled heart tones
options.b: Hypertension, tachycardia, and rapid shallow breathing
options.c: Hypotension, bradycardia, and warm, dry skin
options.d: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations

distractorExplanations.a: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart tones are Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade, not Cushing's triad.
distractorExplanations.b: Cushing's triad has a slow pulse (reflex bradycardia); hypertension with tachycardia suggests pain or sympathetic stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin describes neurogenic shock, not rising intracranial pressure.

options.a: Gently replace the organs, then cover with moist dressing
options.b: Cover organs with moist sterile dressing and occlusive cover
options.c: Cover the organs with dry sterile gauze secured by a tight wrap
options.d: Give small sips of water to treat the developing shock

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing eviscerated organs risks injury and contamination; reduction is a surgical task, so cover them in place.
distractorExplanations.c: Dry gauze adheres to and dries the bowel, and a tight wrap compresses the organs; use moist sterile plus occlusive.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal injury patients are kept NPO because they may need surgery and oral fluids risk vomiting and aspiration.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-010.explanation: Keep organs moist and protected; replacement is a surgical task. Do not push the organs back inside.

options.a: Simple pneumothorax without pressure buildup
options.b: Flail chest with a paradoxical segment
options.c: Tension pneumothorax physiology
options.d: Hemothorax causing hypovolemic shock

distractorExplanations.a: A simple pneumothorax causes dyspnea but not JVD; distended neck veins signal rising intrathoracic pressure.
distractorExplanations.b: Flail chest results from blunt multiple rib fractures and does not explain JVD after a penetrating wound.
distractorExplanations.d: Massive hemothorax causes flat neck veins from blood loss, not distended neck veins.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-011.explanation: Penetrating chest trauma with distress/JVD raises tension pneumothorax concern—rapid transport/ALS. Support ABCs and request ALS per protocol.

options.a: Gently push the organs back in before dressing them
options.b: Cover with a dry sterile dressing secured by tape
options.c: Lay the patient flat with the legs straight to limit the pain
options.d: Cover with a moist sterile dressing and occlusive covering

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing eviscerated organs risks injury and contamination; reduction is a surgical task done in the hospital.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry dressings stick to and dry the organs, and adhesive should not touch them; use moist sterile plus occlusive.
distractorExplanations.c: Flexing the knees (if no spinal injury) relaxes the abdominal wall; straight legs increase tension on the wound.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-012.explanation: Keep organs moist and protected; reduction is a surgical task. Do not push the organs back in.

options.a: Isolated midshaft femur fracture
options.b: Fracture of the pelvis with leg shortening
options.c: Fracture of the knee or lower leg
options.d: Hip dislocation with the leg rotated

distractorExplanations.b: Pelvic fractures are a contraindication because the traction splint pushes against the pelvis.
distractorExplanations.c: Knee and lower-leg injuries are contraindications; traction is for midshaft femur fractures.
distractorExplanations.d: Hip injuries are a contraindication to traction splinting; the hip is splinted in the position found.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-013.explanation: Traction splints stabilize midshaft femurs when criteria are met; pelvis/spine need other care. Confirm there are no contraindications per protocol.

options.a: Hypotension, tachycardia, and warm dry skin
options.b: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations
options.c: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds
options.d: Hypertension, tachycardia, and rapid, shallow respirations

distractorExplanations.c: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds are Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade, not Cushing's triad.
distractorExplanations.d: Cushing's triad has reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia, along with irregular breathing.
distractorExplanations.a: That pattern fits shock more than Cushing.

options.a: Pack the part directly in ice so the tissue stays viable longer
options.b: Bag the part first, then dress the bleeding stump
options.c: Control bleeding, care for the stump, and transport the part
options.d: Submerge the part in sterile saline in a sealed container

distractorExplanations.a: Direct ice contact freezes and damages the tissue; the bagged part is kept cool without touching ice.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong sequence: life-threatening bleeding at the stump is controlled first; the part is handled afterward.
distractorExplanations.d: Soaking waterlogs the tissue and hampers reattachment; the part is wrapped, not immersed.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-trauma-015.explanation: Save the part properly for possible reimplantation while prioritizing life-threatening hemorrhage. Wrap the part cool and dry per protocol, not directly on ice.

options.a: Signs/Symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last oral intake, Events
options.b: Signs/Symptoms, Assessment, Medications, Pertinent negatives, Last vitals, Events
options.c: Symptoms, Allergies, Mechanism, Pulse, Last meal, Exposure
options.d: Signs, Airway, Mental status, Pulse, Lungs, Extremities

distractorExplanations.b: Mixes in non-SAMPLE terms: A is Allergies, P is Past pertinent history, and L is Last oral intake.
distractorExplanations.c: Mechanism, pulse, and exposure belong to trauma assessment; in SAMPLE, M is Medications and P is Past history.
distractorExplanations.d: These are primary survey and physical exam elements, not the components of a SAMPLE history.

options.a: Past medical history and allergies
options.b: Pain/symptom characteristics
options.c: Level of responsiveness
options.d: Mechanism of injury details

distractorExplanations.a: Past history and allergies are gathered with the SAMPLE history, not OPQRST.
distractorExplanations.c: Responsiveness is assessed with AVPU or GCS, not with the OPQRST symptom profile.
distractorExplanations.d: Mechanism of injury is evaluated during scene size-up and trauma assessment, not by OPQRST.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-00.explanation: OPQRST fleshes out the chief complaint symptom profile. The letters stand for Onset, Provocation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, and Time.

options.a: Waiting on scene to see if symptoms resolve as in a TIA
options.b: Giving 324 mg of chewable aspirin before transport
options.c: Rapid transport to an appropriate stroke-capable facility
options.d: Transport to the nearest hospital even if it lacks stroke care

distractorExplanations.a: A TIA cannot be distinguished from a stroke in the field; waiting loses the treatment window.
distractorExplanations.b: Aspirin is an ACS treatment; in stroke a hemorrhagic bleed cannot be excluded in the field and swallowing may be impaired.
distractorExplanations.d: Protocols direct stroke patients to stroke-capable centers when reachable in time, bypassing closer non-stroke hospitals.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-00.explanation: Time-sensitive stroke care needs rapid identification and transport; avoid delays and unsafe oral meds if swallow uncertain. Treatment depends on arrival within time windows.

options.a: A bystander may give consent on behalf of an unresponsive adult
options.b: Unresponsive patients are treated as if they would want life-saving care
options.c: A competent adult agrees to treatment after hearing the risks and benefits
options.d: A parent agrees by phone to treatment of their injured minor child

distractorExplanations.a: Bystanders have no authority to consent; implied consent rests on the presumed wishes of the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes expressed (informed) consent, not implied consent.
distractorExplanations.d: A parent's agreement for a minor is expressed consent by a guardian; implied consent applies when no one can consent.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-00.explanation: Implied consent covers emergency care when a patient cannot decide; competent adults may refuse. This also covers patients impaired to the point they cannot decide.

options.a: Gaining access to the patient through the nearest open door
options.b: Starting a primary survey through the broken window
options.c: Scene safety and personal protective measures
options.d: Stabilizing the patient's cervical spine from the back seat

distractorExplanations.a: Patient access comes after the vehicle is stabilized and hazards are controlled; rushing in endangers rescuers.
distractorExplanations.b: Patient contact comes after hazards are controlled and the vehicle is stabilized.
distractorExplanations.d: Entering before the vehicle is stabilized and hazards are controlled endangers the rescuer.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-00.explanation: Rescuer safety enables sustained patient care; hazards must be controlled. These come before patient access.

options.a: A family member says the patient wouldn't want care
options.b: It was signed by the patient's attorney
options.c: The patient has a terminal illness diagnosis
options.d: It meets local legal requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Verbal statements without valid documentation do not establish a DNR; begin care and contact medical direction.
distractorExplanations.b: A DNR order must be signed by a physician (and patient or proxy) per state law; an attorney's signature does not make it valid.
distractorExplanations.c: A terminal diagnosis alone does not create a DNR; a valid legal order is required.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-00.explanation: Follow legal advance directives/DNR documentation; honor patient wishes when they request care and are competent. It must be presented and verified per protocol.

options.a: Protect from injury, maintain airway, and time the seizure
options.b: Place a bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
options.c: Hold the limbs firmly to stop the convulsions
options.d: Insert an OPA during the seizure to secure the airway

distractorExplanations.b: Objects in the mouth can break teeth, cause airway obstruction, or injure the rescuer; nothing is placed between the teeth.
distractorExplanations.c: Restraining convulsing limbs does not stop the seizure and can cause fractures or soft-tissue injury.
distractorExplanations.d: A clenched jaw and active gag reflex make OPA insertion dangerous; use positioning, suction, or an NPA.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-00.explanation: Protective positioning and airway support; never insert objects into the mouth. Do not force objects into the mouth.

options.a: Red signals may be passed at speed once sirens are on
options.b: Lights/sirens do not guarantee right-of-way
options.c: Seat belts are optional for providers in the back
options.d: Sirens give you right-of-way at intersections

distractorExplanations.a: Most laws require slowing or stopping at red signals and proceeding with due regard for others.
distractorExplanations.d: Other drivers may not hear or yield; emergency vehicles request right-of-way rather than receive it.
distractorExplanations.c: Restraints protect providers.

options.a: Is hypoglycemic but too drowsy to follow commands
options.b: Has hyperglycemia with Kussmaul respirations
options.c: Is hypoglycemic and in the middle of an active seizure
options.d: Is hypoglycemic and can protect their airway/swallow

distractorExplanations.a: Oral glucose requires a patient who can follow commands and swallow; a drowsy patient risks aspiration.
distractorExplanations.c: A seizing patient cannot swallow safely; glucose must be given by another route through ALS.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperglycemia needs different care.

options.a: Promptly to an appropriate stroke-capable facility
options.b: After a full neuro exam is completed on scene
options.c: To the closest hospital even without stroke services
options.d: After waiting several hours to see if symptoms resolve

distractorExplanations.b: A detailed neuro exam can be done en route; delaying transport loses treatment time.
distractorExplanations.c: Protocols direct stroke patients to stroke-capable centers when reachable in time, bypassing closer hospitals.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting wastes the treatment window.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-01.explanation: Time-sensitive stroke care needs rapid transport and hospital alert. Prenotify the hospital when possible.

options.a: Hypotension with a weak, thready pulse and confusion
options.b: Tachycardia with cool, pale, diaphoretic skin
options.c: Bradycardia with warm, dry, flushed skin
options.d: Hypertension with bounding pulses and flushed skin

distractorExplanations.a: Hypotension with a thready pulse and confusion is decompensated (late) shock, not an early sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Bradycardia with warm, dry skin describes neurogenic shock, not early compensated hypovolemic shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypertension is not a shock sign; compensation keeps BP near normal while heart rate rises.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-01.explanation: Compensation often raises HR and causes vasoconstriction signs before hypotension appears. Blood pressure is still near normal at this stage.

options.a: Have a family member sign the refusal for the competent adult
options.b: Record only that the patient refused care, to limit your liability
options.c: Ensure the patient is informed of risks and document thoroughly
options.d: Transport under implied consent if the patient seems unwise

distractorExplanations.a: The competent patient signs their own refusal; family members may witness but cannot sign for them.
distractorExplanations.b: Brief notes increase liability; document risks explained, capacity, and the patient's understanding.
distractorExplanations.d: A competent adult may make an unwise choice; implied consent applies only to patients lacking capacity.

nremt-emt-readiness-check-medical-ops-01.explanation: Informed refusal requires capacity, risk disclosure, and solid documentation. Confirm competence and involve medical direction per protocol.
